variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: A code generation benchmark is a repeatable experiment that asks a model to produce programs, runs those programs against a fixed test contract, and reports how often at least one sampled program succeeds. HumanEval and MBPP are two Python-oriented benchmark collections that make this experiment convenient.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Turn a prompt into executable evidence”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Freeze the manifest
pairs.detail: Version the dataset or product task, prompt, entry point, language image, dependencies, hidden-test policy, decoding settings, and timeout before sampling.
pairs.explanation: Version the dataset or product task, prompt, entry point, language image, dependencies, hidden-test policy, decoding settings, and timeout before sampling.

pairs.label: Sample candidates
pairs.detail: Keep every completion, seed, token count, model revision, and candidate index.
pairs.explanation: Keep every completion, seed, token count, model revision, and candidate index. Do not silently resample failures or select a best-looking answer.

pairs.label: Contain execution
pairs.detail: Parse and execute each candidate in a disposable isolated environment with no ambient credentials, bounded CPU, memory, output, files, processes, and network.
pairs.explanation: Parse and execute each candidate in a disposable isolated environment with no ambient credentials, bounded CPU, memory, output, files, processes, and network.

pairs.label: Score and retain evidence
pairs.detail: Run public and protected tests, retain outcomes and failure classes, calculate the declared pass@k estimator, then report slices, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions.
pairs.explanation: Run public and protected tests, retain outcomes and failure classes, calculate the declared pass@k estimator, then report slices, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. The core invariant is same untrusted workload, same versioned test contract: the score must be reproducible from the frozen task revision, generation settings, sandbox policy, and per-candidate test outcomes.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Freeze the manifest: Version the dataset or product task, prompt, entry point, language image, dependencies, hidden-test policy, decoding settings, and timeout before sampling. Sample candidates: Keep every completion, seed, token count, model revision, and candidate index. Contain execution: Parse and execute each candidate in a disposable isolated environment with no ambient credentials, bounded CPU, memory, output, files, processes, and network. Score and retain evidence: Run public and protected tests, retain outcomes and failure classes, calculate the declared pass@k estimator, then report slices, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: A code generation benchmark is a repeatable experiment that asks a model to produce programs, runs those programs against a fixed test contract, and reports how often at least one sampled program succeeds. HumanEval and MBPP are two Python-oriented benchmark collections that make this experiment convenient.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Use HumanEval and MBPP as narrow lenses”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: HumanEval
pairs.detail: HumanEval presents a Python function signature and docstring, then checks a candidate against tests.
pairs.explanation: HumanEval presents a Python function signature and docstring, then checks a candidate against tests. It is compact and easy to reproduce, but it has only 164 original tasks and is widely discussed.

pairs.label: MBPP
pairs.detail: MBPP contains short natural-language programming problems with solutions and tests.
pairs.explanation: MBPP contains short natural-language programming problems with solutions and tests. It is useful for entry-level behavior, but its task style and minimum test count do not represent a multi-file repository.

pairs.label: What both can reveal
pairs.detail: They can reveal regressions in small algorithmic and implementation tasks when the benchmark revision, prompt, execution harness, and sampling protocol are frozen.
pairs.explanation: They can reveal regressions in small algorithmic and implementation tasks when the benchmark revision, prompt, execution harness, and sampling protocol are frozen.

pairs.label: What neither certifies
pairs.detail: Neither benchmark alone establishes repository navigation, dependency management, secure changes, test maintenance, reviewability, latency, licensing, or production readiness.
pairs.explanation: Neither benchmark alone establishes repository navigation, dependency management, secure changes, test maintenance, reviewability, latency, licensing, or production readiness.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. The core invariant is same untrusted workload, same versioned test contract: the score must be reproducible from the frozen task revision, generation settings, sandbox policy, and per-candidate test outcomes.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. HumanEval: HumanEval presents a Python function signature and docstring, then checks a candidate against tests. variants.prompt: For a task with n generated candidates and c passing candidates, what does pass@k estimate?
options: The probability that at least one of k sampled candidates passes the declared tests
The percentage of source lines that parse successfully
The probability that the first candidate is safe to deploy
The number of hidden tests in the benchmark
variants.explanation: pass@k measures whether a set of k candidates contains a passing solution under the declared test contract. It is not a safety or maintainability score.

variants.prompt: Which condition most directly invalidates an evaluator's security boundary?
options: Generated code runs with a host repository mount and ambient credentials
A protected test checks a boundary input
The report includes a timeout rate
Each candidate has a bounded output limit

The team should remove repository tasks from evaluation

variants.prompt: A protected test suite is flaky on known-good fixtures. What should happen before using it as a release gate?
options: Hold the release and repair or stabilize the verifier
Treat each flaky retry as an independent task
Ignore protected-test outcomes and use visible examples
Increase k until the score passes
variants.explanation: Flaky tests weaken the evidence itself. Repeated candidate executions do not repair a non-deterministic verifier.

variants.prompt: Why can a stronger hidden or adversarial test suite lower an observed pass@k score?
options: It can expose candidates that only fit visible examples
It changes correct programs into incorrect programs
It removes the need for a sandbox
It makes candidate sampling deterministic
variants.explanation: A stronger verifier finds untested failures. The resulting lower score can be more credible because it supports a broader behavioral claim.
